svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 3. Two protocol level additions that no comparison chart lists
svg.desc: On the left, post-quantum hardening. The elliptic curve key exchange used by WireGuard is not quantum resistant, contrary to a common claim; what provides hardening is the optional pre-shared key field, into which a key derived from post-quantum algorithms can be placed. One provider has made this the default on desktop since January 2025, combining a lattice based algorithm standardised by the American standards body with a code based one. On the right, defence against traffic analysis. Even inside a perfect tunnel, the sizes and timing of packets identify which site is being visited, and a defence introduced in 2024 adds cover traffic and regularises packet sizes to disrupt that. A band below notes that both are chosen at the provider rather than by picking a protocol.
svg.text: Figure 3: Two Additions No Comparison Chart Lists
Both are chosen at the provider rather than by picking a protocol, and both address threats the standard comparison does not measure.
POST-QUANTUM HARDENING
and a correction to a claim you will meet often
The claim, and why it is wrong
Guides describe the elliptic curve exchange as quantum resistant.
It is not. It is among the things a quantum computer of sufficient
size would break, which is the entire reason this work exists.
The threat is not the future computer

g.text: It is that traffic captured today can be stored and decrypted
later. Nothing has to exist yet for the recording to be useful,
so anything you send now with a long secrecy requirement is
already exposed to it.

svg.text: What actually provides the hardening

g.text: The protocol has an optional pre-shared key field. A key derived
from post-quantum algorithms is placed into it and combined with
the ordinary exchange, so both must be broken.
One provider has run this by default on desktop since January
2025, pairing the lattice algorithm standardised by the American
standards body with an older code based one.

svg.text: DEFENCE AGAINST TRAFFIC ANALYSIS
the attack a perfect tunnel does not stop
The problem, which Module 3 introduced
Encryption hides the contents. It does not hide how many packets
there were, how large they were, or when they arrived, and those
three together identify which page was loaded with high accuracy.
What a defence does about it

g.text: It sends cover traffic in both directions at unpredictable times
and regularises packet sizes, so the shape of a page load stops
being a shape anybody recognises.
Introduced in 2024, built on an open framework developed with a
university, published and peer reviewed rather than announced.
A second version in 2025 moved the defence from fixed client
rules to instructions negotiated with the server.

svg.text: The costs, stated plainly

g.text: Cover traffic is real traffic. It uses bandwidth you are not
using for anything, and it is offered on a limited set of servers
rather than the whole network.

svg.text: What these two have in common, and why the comparison chart missed both

g.text: Neither is a protocol. Both are things a provider builds on top of one, so they do not appear in a row comparing WireGuard against OpenVPN.
Both address threats the chart does not measure. One is about traffic recorded today and read in fifteen years. The other is about what remains visible after encryption.
And both are things to ask a provider about by name, in the same breath as the questions from Lesson 6.1 about ownership and evidence.

svg.text: A protocol comparison answers which tunnel to open. These two answer what the tunnel still leaks, and how long its contents stay secret.
Neither is urgent for most readers. Both are worth knowing exist, because in five years one of them will be the default everywhere.
